Question: Can agents observe their own execution and flag inefficiencies: repeated exceptions, unnecessary gates, redundant steps, slow integrations? Are improvement proposals generated and routed to process owners?
Response: Yes. The Fleet Manager agent analyses completed workflow telemetry to detect friction. Pattern detection: (1) Repeated exceptions at the same phase across workflows (e.g. works council notification causing 3-day delays in German hires). (2) Unnecessary gates — HITL approvals where the operator always approves without modification (suggests the threshold is too conservative). (3) Redundant steps — phases that produce no meaningful state change. (4) Slow integrations — MCP tool calls with consistently high latency flagged for optimisation. The Fleet Manager composes improvement proposals with supporting evidence (metrics, affected workflow count, estimated impact) and surfaces them on the Control Plane for operator approval. Approved improvements feed into the skill crystallisation pipeline (agent executor → deterministic plain-function executor in the MAF workflow graph) or into new MAF validator executor nodes — process changes are version-controlled as skills + graph definitions in Git, reviewed via APIOps, and promoted through standard lifecycle gates. Runtime agent assembly supports mid-workflow evolution: when Threadlight captures a new pattern from an SME interview during a workflow, it auto-registers the generated skill in Entra Agent ID + API Center (Design state) via the governance-gate callback; a human operator reviews and promotes to Production, and the new capability is live in the next workflow — no redeploy required. This creates a continuous improvement loop: execute -> observe -> propose -> approve -> update -> execute.
Key Technologies: Fleet Manager agent (friction analysis), OTEL telemetry, Control Plane (proposal review), skill crystallisation pipeline, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph evolution
POC Demo: POC2: After 10 completed workflows, Fleet Manager detects works council delay pattern and proposes proactive notification step. Operator approves update.

Question: Can the platform run variant processes across agent cohorts (different prompts, tools, orchestration patterns) with statistical comparison of outcomes?
Response: Yes. The architecture supports A/B testing at two levels. (a) Skill version variants via API Center + APIM traffic splitting — both variants run in production, OTEL + Foundry Evaluator scores collected, Fleet Manager compares. (b) MAF workflow graph variants — two graph definitions (different executor composition, different validator strictness, different orchestration pattern from MAF's sequential/concurrent/handoff/group-chat/Magentic-One set) can run side-by-side with traffic split at the DF activity invocation. Process: (1) Register variants. (2) Configure traffic split (50/50 based on workflow ID hash). (3) Both run in production producing telemetry. (4) Fleet Manager compares outcomes: quality scores, completion time, cost, human override rates, validator failure rates. (5) Statistical comparison surfaced on Control Plane. (6) Operator promotes winning variant to 100%. Requires custom routing/comparison skills — achievable, not a pre-built A/B product. Variant artefacts (both SKILL.md and MAF graph variants) are Git-inspectable; Threadlight (Microsoft delivery accelerator) can capture variant designs from SME interviews for the variant-generation step.
Key Technologies: API Center (variant versioning), APIM (traffic splitting), Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph variants, Foundry Evaluators (quality comparison), Fleet Manager (statistical analysis), Threadlight accelerator

Question: At thousands of simultaneous maturing workflows, how does the platform manage the crystallisation pipeline at scale with dependency tracking?
Response: At scale, the crystallisation pipeline is managed through Azure API Center with dependency tracking. Skills declare their dependencies (which MCP tools they use, which other skills they build upon). API Center maintains the dependency graph. Crystallisation at scale: (1) The Fleet Manager monitors maturity signals across all workflows — consistency of outcomes, override rates, exception frequencies. (2) Crystallisation candidates are prioritised by impact: high-frequency skills with consistent outcomes crystallise first. Crystallised skills auto-register in Entra Agent ID + API Center (Design state) via the governance-gate callback so they are visible for runtime loading; human operator reviews and promotes through API Center lifecycle to Production. (3) API Center lifecycle gates prevent promoting a skill that has unresolved dependencies on non-crystallised components. (4) The CI/CD pipeline runs regression tests against the full dependency graph before promotion. Deprecation tracking: when a crystallised skill is updated, API Center identifies all dependent skills and workflows that may be affected. The Control Plane surfaces dependency impact analysis for operator review.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (dependency graph), Fleet Manager (maturity analysis), CI/CD (regression testing), Control Plane (impact analysis)

Question: When processes change, how are affected agents identified, updated, or retired? Describe dependency tracking across process definitions, tools, and models.
Response: Dependency tracking is managed through Azure API Center and APIM. (1) Skills in API Center declare dependencies: which MCP tools, which models, which other skills they depend on. (2) MCP servers in APIM track which skills/agents consume them. (3) Model deployments in Foundry track which agents use which model versions. When a process changes: (1) Updated skill is registered as a new version in API Center. (2) API Center identifies all downstream skills and workflows that depend on the changed component. (3) Impact analysis is surfaced on the Control Plane — which workflows will be affected, what testing is needed. (4) The deprecated skill version enters 'Deprecated' lifecycle stage — existing running workflows complete on the old version, new workflows use the updated version. (5) Agent 365 (preview today, GA May 2026) supports lifecycle actions (activate, block, delete) for agents that are no longer needed; Entra Agent ID policies automatically update when a dependent skill is deprecated, preventing new workflows from loading deprecated capabilities. Durable Functions timer escalation alerts operators to migrate running workflows. The Fleet Manager monitors deprecated skills still in active use and alerts operators to complete migration.
Key Technologies: Azure API Center (dependency tracking, lifecycle), APIM (consumer tracking), Agent 365 (retirement), Fleet Manager (migration monitoring)
